blocks.text: 1. The Deep Learning Workflow

blocks.alt: Data leads to architecture, then training, then deployment

blocks.text: The Machine Learning Workflow, covered in the traditional Machine Learning course, walked through a repeatable seven-stage sequence: define, collect, explore, prepare, train, evaluate, and deploy. The Deep Learning Workflow follows a genuinely similar overall shape, with several deep-learning-specific stages added in.
Understanding this full sequence previews exactly where every later module in this course actually fits, giving a clear map before diving into any single stage in genuine technical depth.
2. The Full Sequence

blocks.alt: The workflow moves from preparing data through designing, training, evaluating, and deploying

blocks.text: The full Deep Learning workflow moves through seven broad stages. It starts with defining the problem and gathering data, then preprocessing that data into a network-ready format, then designing the network's actual architecture.

From there, it moves to choosing a loss function and an optimizer, training the network, evaluating and tuning it, and finally deploying and monitoring it once it is genuinely ready for real-world use. Each of these seven stages gets covered across the modules that make up the rest of this course.

blocks.text: 3. Designing the Network Architecture

Designing the network architecture is a genuinely new stage compared to the traditional Machine Learning workflow, where choosing an algorithm was often a comparatively simpler decision. How many layers a network should have, and how wide each individual layer should be, is covered in depth in Neural Network Fundamentals, the very next module in this course.

Which specific architecture family actually fits a given problem also matters considerably, Convolutional Neural Networks for image data, Transformers for text, each covered in their own dedicated modules later in this course, since different architecture families are specifically built to handle different kinds of raw, unstructured data well.
4. Choosing a Loss Function and an Optimizer

blocks.alt: A loss function pairs with an optimizer

blocks.text: Choosing a loss function defines exactly what wrong actually means for a given problem, a specific, mathematical definition covered in genuine depth in the Loss Functions module later in this course.

Choosing an optimizer defines exactly how the network's weights actually get adjusted during training, covered in full in the Backpropagation and Optimization module immediately following Loss Functions. These two choices together shape essentially everything about how a network actually learns.
5. The Training Loop

blocks.alt: A forward pass computes loss, a backward pass updates weights

blocks.text: Training a deep network follows a repeated loop. A forward pass sends the input flowing through the network, producing a prediction, and computing the loss compares that prediction directly against the actual, known correct answer.

A backward pass then calculates how each individual weight across the entire network actually contributed to that loss, covered in full mathematical depth in the Backpropagation and Optimization module ahead, and updating weights adjusts each one to reduce the loss, using whatever optimizer was chosen in the previous stage. This loop then repeats continuously across the training data.
6. Epochs and Batches

blocks.alt: A batch is part of a full epoch

blocks.text: Two genuinely important pieces of training vocabulary come up constantly throughout the rest of this course. A batch is a small group of training examples processed together in one single training step, rather than processing the entire dataset all at once.

An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training dataset, meaning every single training example has been used exactly once. Training typically involves many epochs, each one made up of many batches, a structure covered in far more practical depth in the Training Deep Networks module later in this course.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: These two terms, batch and epoch, appear constantly throughout the rest of this course. Getting comfortable with the distinction now will make the more technical modules ahead considerably easier to follow.

blocks.text: 7. Watching for Overfitting

blocks.alt: Train loss falling while validation loss rises signals overfitting

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the generalization goal already covered in the Supervised Learning topic from the traditional Machine Learning course. A deep network, with its genuinely large number of learnable parameters, is especially prone to overfitting, memorizing its training data rather than learning a pattern that actually generalizes.

Regularization Techniques, an entire dedicated module later in this course, exists specifically to address this exact risk, covering several concrete, practical techniques for keeping a deep network's learning genuinely generalizable rather than merely memorized.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Overfitting is worth watching for throughout every single training run in this course, not just as a one-time concept covered here. It is one of the most common, recurring practical challenges in real Deep Learning work.

blocks.text: 8. A Practical, Deep-Learning-Specific Consideration: Hardware

This connects back to the compute ingredient already covered in the Why Deep Learning Works topic. Training on a CPU alone is often impractically slow for anything beyond a genuinely tiny network, given how much matrix computation deep network training actually requires.

Training on a GPU, or a cloud-based GPU instance, is the practical default for any genuinely serious Deep Learning project today, a hardware consideration that simply does not come up in the same way throughout most of the traditional Machine Learning course.

blocks.text: 9. Deployment, Previewed

blocks.alt: A trained model is covered here, Production Deep Learning comes later

blocks.text: This connects back to Model Deployment, already covered in genuine depth in the traditional Machine Learning course. Deep Learning deployment shares the exact same core ideas, serialization, an inference pipeline, ongoing monitoring, all covered in that earlier module.

But it also adds deep-learning-specific concerns on top of those shared foundations, covered in full in Production Deep Learning, a dedicated module later in this course, addressing considerations like model size and inference speed that matter especially for large, deep networks specifically.
10. Why This Full Sequence Matters

Walking through this full sequence before diving into any single stage keeps each deeply technical module ahead genuinely connected to the bigger picture, exactly the same reasoning already applied in the traditional Machine Learning course's own workflow topic.

Every specific technique covered across the many modules still ahead, a particular activation function, a particular architecture, a particular regularization method, has a clear, specific place within this seven-stage sequence, worth returning to mentally whenever a new, deeply technical topic risks feeling disconnected from the overall picture.
11. Worked Example
The example below walks through a small but complete version of this workflow, from raw data through a trained, evaluated neural network.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Stage 1: problem defined, data gathered (simulated here)
rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X_raw = rng.normal(size=(800, 10))
y = (X_raw[:, 0] + X_raw[:, 3] - X_raw[:, 7] > 0).astype(int)

# Stage 2: preprocessing
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_raw)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

# Stage 3 and 4: architecture, loss, and optimizer chosen via MLPClassifier's parameters
model = MLPClassifier(
    hidden_layer_sizes=(32, 16),  # architecture: two hidden layers
    max_iter=300,                 # training epochs
    batch_size=32,                # batch size
    random_state=42
)

# Stage 5: training
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Stage 6: evaluation
test_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
print(f"Test accuracy: {test_accuracy:.2%}")
print(f"Training completed in {model.n_iter_} epochs")

# Stage 7: deployment and monitoring would follow, covered later in this course
print("\nModel ready; stages 1 through 6 of the Deep Learning workflow are complete for this example")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example uses scikit-learn's MLPClassifier for simplicity. Real Deep Learning projects typically use a dedicated framework like PyTorch, covered in its own module in this broader course series, offering considerably more control over each of the seven stages.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: The Deep Learning Workflow follows a familiar shape to traditional Machine Learning, with deep-learning-specific stages added.
The full sequence: define and gather data, preprocess, design architecture, choose loss and optimizer, train, evaluate, deploy.
Designing the architecture, choosing layer count and family, is a genuinely new stage covered in modules ahead.
A loss function defines what wrong means; an optimizer defines how weights actually get adjusted.
The training loop repeats: forward pass, compute loss, backward pass, and weight updates.
A batch is a group of examples processed together; an epoch is one complete pass through the training data.
A deep network's many parameters make it especially prone to overfitting, addressed by Regularization Techniques ahead.
GPU training is the practical default for any serious Deep Learning project, given the scale of computation required.
